title: Make scarcity real, then make the choice clear.
dek: In Cialdini's chapter on scarcity, limited availability raises perceived value and threatens freedom of choice; the practical discipline is to distinguish genuine constraints from manufactured urgency.

marginNote.label: Apprenticeship Note
marginNote.body: Scarcity works twice: it makes the option feel more valuable and makes delay feel like a loss of freedom. Use it only when the constraint is real and legible.

canon.heading: Scarcity changes the value of the choice—and the feeling of delay.
canon.standfirst: Read Chapter 7, "Scarcity: The Rule of the Few," from Robert B. Cialdini's Influence, on PDF pages 187-213. Cialdini shows how limited availability and threatened freedom increase desire, while warning that arousal can make people decide before they think.
canon.readerIntro: Read this chapter as both a persuasion lesson and a defensive checklist. Mark the moments where scarcity changes perceived value, where a restriction creates reactance, and where emotional arousal should trigger a pause.

blocks.label: 01 / Limited availability raises value
paragraphs: Cialdini opens with opportunities that become attractive because they may soon disappear. Scarcity supplies a shortcut for value: if access is limited, the option feels more worth having.
The effect is strongest when the loss is vivid and the person has already imagined possessing the thing.

blocks.label: 02 / Freedom makes the constraint bite
paragraphs: A restriction does more than reduce supply. It threatens freedom of choice, producing psychological reactance and a desire to restore the option before it is taken away.
This explains why a newly restricted option can become more desirable than it was when freely available.

blocks.label: 03 / Competition intensifies arousal
paragraphs: Deadlines, limited numbers, and visible competition can compress attention and turn a considered choice into a contest against loss or another buyer.
The chapter's practical warning is to treat feverish urgency as a signal to stop, regain perspective, and inspect the real alternatives.

blocks.label: 04 / Use the principle without manufacturing it
paragraphs: Scarcity is persuasive when the limitation is genuine, relevant, and clearly communicated. False scarcity can create action, but it damages trust and trains people to resist the offer.
The useful commercial question is not how to make anything feel rare; it is which real constraint makes timely action valuable to the customer.

passageAnchors: The way to love anything is to realize that it might be lost
opportunities seem more valuable to us when their availability is limited
the idea of potential loss plays a large role in human decision making
As soon as we feel the tide of emotional arousal ... we should use that rise ... as a signal to stop short
closeReading: Which example shows scarcity changing the perceived value of an option that was previously uninteresting?
Where does Cialdini distinguish the scarcity of the thing from the threatened freedom to choose it?
How do limited numbers, deadlines, and competition differ in the kind of pressure they create?
What signs of emotional arousal does the chapter offer as a cue to pause before deciding?
Which real constraint in one of your offers could be stated honestly, and what manufactured urgency should be removed?

principle.heading: Make the real constraint legible; protect the decision.
principle.body: Scarcity can make a valuable option easier to choose, but it can also make a rushed choice feel inevitable. Name the genuine limit, show why timing matters, and give the customer enough room to decide with perspective.
principle.example: A workshop has 12 seats because each participant receives live critique. Publish the actual seat limit, explain the consequence of late registration, and keep the price and curriculum visible so the deadline clarifies a real constraint rather than hiding the offer.
principle.practice: Audit one current offer. Write down every scarcity cue, label each as real or manufactured, and replace one vague urgency claim with the concrete constraint, customer consequence, and fair decision window.

fieldNotes.title: OpenAI expands frontier AI access to every level of government
fieldNotes.whatHappened: OpenAI and the U.S. General Services Administration announced a 27-month agreement offering eligible federal, state, local, and tribal governments free ChatGPT Enterprise licenses and 50% off usage, alongside cyber-defense access and enablement.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The offer makes a real constraint—public-sector adoption capacity—legible through pricing, training, spend controls, and a defined term. It is a useful contrast with vague AI urgency: the value proposition is attached to a concrete window and operating support.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether a time-bounded subsidy plus onboarding produces durable workflows after the offer period, rather than only a burst of pilots.

fieldNotes.title: Cadbury turns a five-item object into a generosity campaign
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Cadbury launched its largest U.S. campaign with Luar and Nylon around a crystal-studded clutch sized for sharing XL chocolate bars; five clutches were made, with a later sweepstakes for consumers.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The scarcity is specific and believable because the object is a campaign prop, not falsely limited inventory. The constraint gives the generosity platform a memorable symbol while the broader product remains available.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether the scarce object earns attention for the brand idea or becomes the entire story, separating useful rarity from a disconnected collectible stunt.

fieldNotes.title: Meta positions Muse as a shopping agent, not another destination
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Meta introduced Muse, a personal AI agent, while Stripe said its Link wallet can help Muse shop across the internet; the product announcement frames the agent as acting on a person’s behalf across tasks.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The interface shift moves the decision from browsing a catalog to delegating a choice. That raises the importance of explicit limits, approvals, and explainable timing—otherwise convenience can quietly become pressure.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch where users retain control over merchant choice, price ceilings, substitutions, and final approval when an agent turns a recommendation into a purchase.

fieldNotes.title: Stripe gives an AI agent a bounded way to spend
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Stripe announced that Meta integrated Link’s agent wallet with Muse. Consumers approve the transaction total in chat; for businesses outside Link, the wallet issues a single-use virtual card scoped to the approved purchase.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The spending boundary is concrete: a specific purchase, a visible total, and a single-use credential. That is how agentic convenience can preserve choice instead of turning delegated shopping into an uninspectable commitment.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether agent checkout keeps approval, merchant identity, substitutions, and total cost legible at the moment a recommendation becomes an order.

tweets.author: Ram Ahluwalia CFA, Lumida
tweets.title: A product fragment on turning capability into behavior
tweets.summary: This fragment is useful because it names the behavioral question behind a new capability. The important test is not whether the feature is impressive, but whether it changes a repeated workflow enough for the user to adopt it.
tweets.text:
So, the Navier Stokes equation was solved by AI.

BUT, it was solved by brute force.

It was not solved by an original insight.

Einstein’s reframing of gravity from a pulling force to a geometric (curvature) effect of space and time was truly original
and mindblowing.

It was one single insight.

The prediction of time dilation and twin paradoxes was also borne of one single insight.

As compute gets cheaper we will solve more brute force problems.

(Isn’t ‘brute force’ another word for experimentation?)

Physics has the experimental science aspect - where AI will excel.

Then there are the theoretical physicists.

Still, we are not anywhere close to the kind of theoretical physics insight that Einstein or Newton generated.

If AI can reconcile quantum theory and general relativity, then AGI is here.

That is another test for AGI.

That test won’t pass in the next 5 years is my view, and probably a lot longer.

signals.tweetHeading: One fragment from the timeline worth carrying into the work.

output.heading: Use scarcity to clarify timing, not to steal deliberation.
output.body: Find the real limit in one offer, make its consequence clear, and preserve enough perspective for the customer to choose well.
